title: Tools
text:
NotePlanned for spring 2027



These tools will run in your browser. No sign up needed.



Battery revenue calculator: choose power, duration and efficiency, see what a battery would have earned from day ahead price spreads.
Imbalance cost calculator: see what forecast errors cost a plant at real imbalance prices.
Bill estimator: see how a household bill splits into energy, network and taxes.
GÖP or GİP explorer: compare day ahead and intraday prices by hour.

A market bidding game is planned as a separate app.

title: Legislation tree
section: How the instruments rank, with the Turkish terms
text:
How the instruments rank, with the Turkish terms
Turkish rules form a ladder. A rule lower on the ladder must rest on one above it and cannot contradict it. The list reads from the top. This is a reading guide for the timeline, not a legal text; how binding a communiqué or a procedure is depends on its own legal basis.










Rank
English
Turkish
Who issues it
Example in this section




1
Constitution
Anayasa
Constituent power (referendum)
Article 124 lets public bodies issue regulations; the Constitutional Court (Anayasa Mahkemesi) checks laws against it


2
Ratified international agreement
Uluslararası antlaşma
President signs, Parliament approves
Energy and interconnection agreements (none in the timeline yet)


3
Law
Kanun
Parliament (TBMM)
Law 6446, the Electricity Market Law (Elektrik Piyasası Kanunu)


3
Decree law (until 2018)
Kanun Hükmünde Kararname (KHK)
Council of Ministers, with delegated authority
KHK 703 (2018)


3
Presidential decree (from 2018)
Cumhurbaşkanlığı Kararnamesi (CBK)
President
None in the timeline yet


4
Presidential decision (before 2018: Council of Ministers decision)
Cumhurbaşkanı Kararı (before 2018: Bakanlar Kurulu Kararı, BKK)
President (before 2018, the Council of Ministers)
Decision 3453 on renewable support prices; BKK 2015/8317 on transition periods


5
Regulation
Yönetmelik
A ministry or public body, here mostly EPDK, to apply a law
Balancing and Settlement Regulation (DUY), Licence Regulation


6
Communiqué
Tebliğ
The same bodies; details and methods under a regulation
EPDK’s revenue regulation and tariff communiqués (not yet in the timeline)


6
Procedures and principles
Usul ve Esaslar
EPDK, adopted by board decision
The price limits procedure under the DUY


7
Board decision
Kurul Kararı
EPDK Board (Enerji Piyasası Düzenleme Kurulu)
Decision 8965-2, price limit decisions, free consumer limit decisions



Two kinds of board decision matter. A regulatory decision (düzenleyici işlem) sets a rule for the whole market, such as the price limits or the free consumer limit. An individual decision (bireysel işlem) applies to one company, such as granting a licence or a fine. Both are called a Kurul Kararı, so the timeline names the subject, not just the number.

Stages and states of a text








English
Turkish
What it means here




Bill
Kanun teklifi
A proposal to Parliament. Since 2018 it comes from members of parliament; the older term for a government bill is kanun tasarısı


Draft
Taslak
A text published for comment before adoption; EPDK usually asks for opinions (görüş) on regulation drafts


Adoption date
Kabul tarihi
The day Parliament passed a law


Publication
Yayım
Printing in the Official Gazette (Resmî Gazete, RG); the date most regulations are cited by


Duplicate issue
Mükerrer
An extra issue of the same gazette number, often used for urgent texts


Entry into force
Yürürlüğe giriş
The day the text applies, which can differ from publication


Amendment
Değişiklik (also tadil)
A text that changes another; the amended text keeps its number


Provisional article
Geçici madde
A transition rule inside a law or regulation


Additional article
Ek madde
An article added later, usually numbered with an extra mark


Consolidated text
Güncel metin or birleştirilmiş metin
The current text with all amendments included


First, old, latest version
İlk, eski, son versiyon (or hal)
EPDK’s labels for versions on its pages


Repealed
Mülga
No longer in force; EPDK keeps lists of repealed texts


Annulment
İptal
A court removes a text: the Constitutional Court for laws, the Council of State (Danıştay) for regulations


Stay of execution
Yürütmenin durdurulması
A court suspends a text while the case is pending


Legal basis
Dayanak
The article of a higher text that authorises a regulation


Licence, pre-licence
Lisans, önlisans
The permits EPDK grants; the pre-licence comes first


Legislation
Mevzuat
All of these texts together



Terms for the institutions are on the institutions page.

title: Market timeline
text:
47 changes that shaped how the Turkish power market works today, from the state monopoly to storage and remote control. Each card has one tag: Liberalisation (how the market was opened up), Power market (how electricity is priced, traded and settled), Generation (who may build and on what terms), Grid and system operation and Market transition (renewable reforms, storage, certificates, carbon pricing and electric vehicles). Laws and regulations appear only as small tags on a card, and each card says where it was read. The method page explains the source labels and what was not read, and institutions says who does what.

1970s1970LiberalisationA state monopolyTürkiye Elektrik Kurumu (TEK) was created with a monopoly over generation, transmission, distribution and supply.Electricity Authority Law (1312)Source: Law-firm sector report1980s1980s–90sLiberalisationPrivate investors enter through build-operate-transferBefore the market law, private participation came through build-operate-transfer, build-operate and transfer-of-operating-rights models, inside a sector still run by the state utility.Source: Law-firm sector report1990s1994LiberalisationThe state utility is splitTEK was divided into TEAŞ (generation and transmission) and TEDAŞ (distribution), which became the national distribution monopoly.Source: Law-firm sector report2000sMar 2001LiberalisationA regulator and the first market lawThe Electricity Market Law (4628) created the independent regulator EPDK and introduced licences, the eligible consumer and a market financial settlement centre. According to the EPİAŞ handbook, the state utility TEAŞ was split at the same time into generation (EÜAŞ), transmission (TEİAŞ) and wholesale companies.Electricity Market Law (4628)Source: Official text reproduced, EPİAŞ market handbook2001Grid and system operationTEİAŞ (TSO) createdTEİAŞ was formed as the state transmission company and the system operator (TSO) when the state utility was unbundled. It owns and operates the national transmission grid and is responsible for balancing and load dispatch.Source: Law-firm note on TEİAŞ, EPİAŞ market handbookMay 2001LiberalisationA gas market lawThe Natural Gas Market Law (4646), enacted on 2 May 2001, set the framework for a regulated, competitive gas market under the same regulator, EPDK.Natural Gas Market Law (4646)Source: Thesis abstract on gas regulation2001–2026LiberalisationConsumers gain the right to choose, in stepsThe 2001 law let consumers above 9 million kWh a year choose their supplier, and EPDK has set the limit every year since. The aim was a soft landing: the 2004 strategy froze the limit at 7.8 GWh until 2009 and tied it to transition contracts covering at least 85% of forecast load for those who could not yet choose, with full opening targeted for 2011. The limit then fell to 3,600 kWh in 2016, 1,200 kWh in 2021 and 500 kWh in 2026.Electricity Market Law (4628)Source: Competition Authority sector report, News report, 2026 limit2003Power marketFinancial settlement beginsThe 2003 Financial Settlement Communiqué started pricing the electricity that autoproducers fed into and took from the system, in three time periods, according to the EPİAŞ handbook. A legal commentary dates the opening of the electricity market to 1 April 2003.Source: EPİAŞ market handbook, Legal commentaryMar 2004LiberalisationStrategy for the 2000s: privatise distribution firstA strategy paper set the order of reform: sell distribution first, then generation, create portfolio generation companies and replace cost-based tariffs with an equalisation mechanism.Source: Strategy paper, Ministry copy, TEPAV note summarising itNov 2004Power marketFirst balancing and settlement rulesThe first Balancing and Settlement Regulation (DUY), of 3 November 2004, named PMUM as market operator and MYTM as system operator. Balancing and settlement under it began on 1 August 2006, with hourly instructions priced at the system marginal price and monthly settlement.Balancing and Settlement Regulation (DUY)Source: EPİAŞ market handbookMay 2005GenerationThe first renewable support lawThe Renewable Energy Law (5346) introduced the YEK certificate and a support mechanism for renewable generation. The fixed price schedule per source came later, with the 2010 amendment.Renewable Energy Law (5346)Source: Official text reproduced2009–2013LiberalisationDistribution is privatisedTürkiye's distribution network was divided into 21 regions, and 20 of them were sold to private owners between 2009 and 2013 for about 12.7 billion USD in total, the first transfer (Başkent) on 28 January 2009 and the last (Toroslar) on 30 September 2013. The buyers were about ten large construction and energy groups, some holding several regions; only Kayseri stayed with its municipality.Source: News report, News analysis of the ownersDec 2009Power marketDay-ahead planning and hourly settlementFrom 1 December 2009 the final DUY brought a day-ahead planning step that the handbook calls the first step towards the day-ahead market. Settlement became hourly and consumers began to forecast their own consumption.Balancing and Settlement Regulation (DUY)Source: EPİAŞ market handbook, Official text reproduced2010s2010–2015Grid and system operationJoined to the European gridIn September 2010 the Turkish grid began a one-year trial of parallel operation with the continental European system, over two 400 kV lines to Bulgaria and one to Greece. Per the handbook, a permanent agreement followed on 14 April 2015.Source: Trade press, 2010, EPİAŞ market handbook2011GenerationYEKDEM: fixed prices, shared costAn amendment to the Renewable Energy Law (6094), of 29 December 2010, gave renewable plants a fixed price per source for ten years: 7.3 US cents per kWh for hydro and wind, 10.5 for geothermal and 13.3 for solar and biomass. Suppliers pay the cost together, in proportion to their sales, and the market operator calculates the total; the handbook dates the mechanism's start to 1 December 2011.Renewable Energy Law (5346), amended by (6094)Source: Official text reproduced, EPİAŞ market handbook2011GenerationUnlicensed generation startsPeople and companies that generate renewable electricity for their own consumption need no licence, and can sell any surplus they feed into the grid at the schedule prices for ten years; the supplier of last resort must buy it.Renewable Energy Law (5346), Art. 6/ASource: Official text reproducedDec 2011Power marketThe day-ahead market startsThe day-ahead market (GÖP) began on 1 December 2011 and sets the hourly day-ahead price (PTF). The collateral and advance payment system started at the same time.Source: EPİAŞ brochureMar 2013LiberalisationA new main market lawThe Electricity Market Law (6446) became the market's main law. It brought in pre-licences, defined which small plants need no licence and gave EPİAŞ its legal basis.Electricity Market Law (6446)Source: Official text reproducedMar 2013GenerationPre-licencesA pre-licence lets a developer obtain the permits, approvals and land rights needed to start building before the generation licence is issued. It lasts up to 24 months, extendable by half, requires a guarantee letter, and without the permits no licence follows.Electricity Market Law (6446), Art. 6Source: Official text reproducedMar 2013GenerationUnlicensed generation written into the market lawThe Electricity Market Law (6446) lists the activities that need no licence: renewable plants up to 1 MW, plants that use all their output on site, municipal waste plants, micro-cogeneration and emergency generator sets. Storage and demand-side participation were added to the list in 2018.Electricity Market Law (6446), Art. 14Source: Official text reproduced, Law text (2018 addition)2015Power marketEPİAŞ takes over market operationA separate market operator, EPİAŞ, was founded in March 2015 and received a 49-year market operation licence on 1 September 2015. It took over the day-ahead and intraday markets and imbalance settlement, while TEİAŞ kept the balancing power market.Electricity Market Law (6446)Source: News report, EPİAŞ market handbookJul 2015Power marketIntraday market opensThe intraday market (GİP) opened on 1 July 2015, first inside TEİAŞ, and passed to EPİAŞ with the September licence.Source: EPİAŞ market handbookJan 2016Grid and system operationTEİAŞ becomes an ENTSO-E observerTEİAŞ states it became ENTSO-E's first and only observer member on 14 January 2016. For this site it matters because ENTSO-E data covers only Bulgaria, Greece and Georgia for Türkiye. The handbook says the first observer agreement ended in January 2019 and a new one ran from 2023 to 30 June 2026; a 14 July 2026 meeting discussed continuing it, and no later agreement was found.Source: TEİAŞ page, EPİAŞ market handbookMar 2016Power marketMarket data goes publicThe Transparency Platform started publishing market data on 14 March 2016. It is the main data source for this site.Source: EPİAŞ market handbookJun 2016Grid and system operationGrid for renewable resource areasAn amendment to the Electricity Market Law (6719) made TEİAŞ responsible for building the transmission lines that renewable resource areas need, in line with the plants' commissioning schedules.Electricity Market Law (6446), amended by (6719)Source: Law textJun 2016Market transitionRenewable resource areasAn amendment to the Electricity Market Law (6719) lets the state designate renewable energy resource areas (YEKA) and award them in competition; the winning price is paid under the support mechanism for a period set in the tender.Electricity Market Law (6446), amended by (6719)Source: Law textMay 2017GenerationCompetition for wind and solar grid capacityWhen applications for a grid region exceed the capacity TEİAŞ announces, or several apply for the same site, TEİAŞ runs a competition. The lowest offer in US cents per kWh wins and may not exceed the schedule price for the source.Source: Regulation text (supplied)Aug 2017Market transitionFirst large wind tenderThe first resource-area tender, for 1,000 MW of wind, was won by Siemens Gamesa, Kalyon and Türkerler, according to press reports.Source: News reportSep 2018Power marketA spot gas marketEPİAŞ opened the Spot Natural Gas Market on 1 September 2018, an organised market where gas shippers trade with each other around the clock and correct their imbalances.Source: EPİAŞ brochureMay 2019GenerationUnlicensed rules rewrittenThe Unlicensed Electricity Generation Regulation of 12 May 2019 keeps renewable plants up to 1 MW, or the upper limit the President sets, licence-free. Production can be offset against consumption within the same distribution region, with exceptions.Unlicensed Electricity Generation RegulationSource: Official text reproduced2020sNov 2020Market transitionCertificates for renewable originThe market operator issues YEK-G certificates, one per MWh, as proof that supplied electricity came from renewable sources, and they can be traded.Renewable Energy Guarantee Certificate (YEK-G) RegulationSource: Official text reproduced2020–2021Market transitionSupport prices move to liraAn amendment to the Renewable Energy Law (7257), of December 2020, lets the President set support prices for plants commissioned after 31 December 2020, and Presidential decision 3453 (January 2021) set them in lira for plants commissioned from 1 July 2021 to the end of 2025. Press reports give 40 kuruş per kWh for hydro, 32 for wind and solar and 54 for geothermal.Renewable Energy Law (5346), amended by (7257)Source: News report, Law-firm noteJun 2021Power marketA futures market for powerThe Power Futures Market (VEP) opened on 1 June 2021, giving traders a place to hedge months and years ahead. title: Methodology
text:
Conventions

Time: all timestamps are in Türkiye time (UTC+3). Each hour is labelled by its start, so 14:00 covers 14:00 to 15:00.
Currency: prices are in TRY per MWh, as published. Comparisons across years or countries also use the EUR and USD prices published by EPİAŞ, because TRY inflation distorts long TRY series.
Averages: every average states whether it is simple (each hour weighted equally) or volume weighted.

title: Methodology
text:
Definitions

PTF (Piyasa Takas Fiyatı): the day ahead market clearing price.
SMF (Sistem Marjinal Fiyatı): the system marginal price from the balancing market.

title: Electricity prices
section: Price limits: a cap and a floor
text:
Price limits: a cap and a floor
Offers and prices in the day-ahead market must stay between a minimum and a maximum set by the regulator, EPDK. The minimum has always been zero. The maximum has changed many times; the balancing market (SMF) works under the same limits. Both are published in the Official Gazette.
Why a cap? The decisions we read state the limit but not the reasoning, so this part is our reading of press reports and of the market’s structure. A cap limits what one hour can cost buyers when supply is tight, when a few large plants set the price, or when gas costs jump with the exchange rate. Until spring 2022 the cap followed a formula: three times the trailing twelve-month weighted average PTF, and at most 2,000 TL/MWh, so it rose as prices rose. Since 1 April 2022 it is a fixed amount in lira that the board changes by decision.
Why a floor at zero? Bids below zero are not accepted, so the price cannot go negative. Most European day-ahead markets allow negative prices, with a harmonised minimum of −500 EUR/MWh in the coupled EU market at the time of writing (a regulatory limit that can change). In Türkiye the decisions simply state a minimum of 0. When must-run and renewable output exceeds demand, the price sits at zero, so zero-price hours show that there is a surplus but not how large it is.
What the limits do to the data. At the cap or the floor the price stops carrying information about scarcity or surplus: it is cut off, not observed. Averages, spreads and volatility measures are therefore likely to be smaller than they would be without limits, and a cap that is hit often shapes the whole price distribution; the chart below shows how often.


In the last 12 months, PTF reached the cap in at least one hour on 45% of days (164 of 365). The cap in force on 13 November 2026 is 4,500 TL/MWh, about 81 EUR/MWh at the average exchange rate of the last 30 days. At its highest in euros (Sep 2022) it was about 272 EUR/MWh. Increases in the lira cap have not kept pace with the lira’s fall, so the cap is lower in euros than it was.

title: Generation and demand
section: Generation the real-time data does not see
text:
Generation the real-time data does not see
Many small plants, mostly rooftop and other unlicensed solar, are not metered by the system operator in real time. Part of what they produce is used on the spot by the building or factory that owns them, so it never travels through the grid; the rest goes into the local distribution network. Either way it is missing from the generation data above, yet it lowers the demand that the rest of the power system has to serve.
Since 30 December 2020 real-time consumption includes the demand these plants meet. That gives a way to estimate them: consumption minus metered generation minus net imports. In the data this estimate is close to zero at night and follows the sun by day, which is what unmetered solar would do. It also picks up any other unmetered generation and metering differences, so it is an estimate, not a measurement. It cannot be built for earlier years, because consumption did not include these plants then.


                            
                                            




In October 2026 the estimate was 2.7 TWh, or 10% of reported consumption, against 9% in October 2025. Over the last 12 complete months it ranged from 4% (January) to 14% (June): it follows the sun, not demand. As a check, EPİAŞ publishes its own series for unlicensed plants (“YEKDEM Lisanssız Üretim Miktarı”, the settlement feed-in values of unlicensed plants within YEKDEM), with a delay of some months. In the 57 months from January 2022 to September 2026 for which both exist, our estimate is between 88% and 117% of that series (median 100%). The estimate is therefore close to EPİAŞ’s own figure, and it is available as soon as consumption and generation are.

title: Balancing instructions
text:
What the instructions are
After the day-ahead and intraday markets close, the system operator (TEİAŞ) keeps supply and demand in balance in real time. When the system is short of energy it orders plants to produce more, an up-regulation instruction (YAL). When the system has too much it orders plants to produce less, a down-regulation instruction (YAT). Every instruction carries a label. According to the Balancing and Settlement Regulation, label 0 is for balancing energy, label 1 for relieving constraints in the transmission grid, and label 2 for ancillary services such as frequency control. We use the label published with each instruction; we have yet to confirm with EPİAŞ that the published code is this label.
The grid-constraint label matters for cost. A plant ordered up for a constraint is paid the price it offered, whatever the day-ahead price was. The share of instructions carrying label 1 therefore shows how much of balancing is about where electricity is produced, not about how much. Volumes below are the energy instructed; the bottom of the page shows how much was delivered.

title: One price, two Türkiyes
text:
Türkiye’s cheapest electricity comes from the centre and the east of the country, while most of it is used in the northwest. In 2026 the lines between the two were full on the very days when power was cheapest.
I first saw this in the balancing data on this site. In May 2026 the day-ahead price averaged €11/MWh and 214 hours cleared at zero. In the same month TEİAŞ ordered 1.93 TWh of up-regulation with the grid-constraint label: 98% of all up-regulation, against 2% over the whole of 2025. EPİAŞ’s congestion cost for May was 5.8 billion TL, and 95% of it went to plants in Marmara provinces. Why would the grid be under the most pressure when electricity was plentiful and cheap? That is the question I tried to answer.
Figure 1: Monthly average day-ahead price (top) and up-regulation ordered with the grid-constraint label (bottom). Source: EPİAŞ Şeffaflık Platformu, TR Power Lab.
The short answer is geography. On low-price days, solar in Central Anatolia and hydro in the east push large volumes of power west. The lines into Thrace and Istanbul cannot carry all of it. To keep the grid within its limits, TEİAŞ orders cheap plants in Anatolia to produce less and pays more expensive plants close to the load to produce more. The market price that day is low, but the cost of actually delivering the power is not.
SHURA’s report on locational marginal pricing, published in June 2026, points to the same place. It describes Thrace as the main regional bottleneck in the system: one of the country’s largest load centres, connected to the rest of the grid through limited transmission capacity.

title: One price, two Türkiyes
section: One price for the whole country
text:
One price for the whole country
Every day EPİAŞ clears one hourly market clearing price (PTF) for all of Türkiye, a country of more than 80 million people and 81 provinces, and that price ignores transmission limits. Bids close at 12:30 the day before. Offers are ranked from cheapest to most expensive and matched with demand. The whole country is one bidding zone, so a megawatt-hour in Hakkari is worth the same as one in Edirne.
The day-ahead market (GÖP) is where the reference price is set. In 2024 and 2025 it cleared about 230 TWh a year, roughly two-thirds of consumption; so far in 2026 the figure is 59%. Bilateral contracts and the balancing market are priced off it too.
Think of milk. Say Türkiye drinks 100 million litres a day, produced everywhere from Hakkari to Edirne, and two-thirds of it is sold at a single national price. That price ignores how the milk reaches people: fuel, tolls, and how many trucks can get into Istanbul, where demand is highest and local production is small. When the trucks are full, someone has to buy milk at a premium near Istanbul and pour away cheap milk in the east. Electricity works the same way, except that, unlike milk, nobody can go without it, and a shortage can cost millions of dollars. The transmission lines are the trucks. Congestion is what happens when the trucks are full, or when there are not enough of them at busy times in busy places.
A single price has a real advantage: every generator competes in one large, liquid market. What it leaves out is regional supply and demand and the limits of the grid. Those costs do not disappear. They move out of the market price and into TEİAŞ’s redispatch bill.

title: One price, two Türkiyes
section: Where power is made and where it is used
text:
Where power is made and where it is used
Demand is concentrated in the northwest, solar in Central Anatolia and hydro in the east. Istanbul alone produced 29.2% of Türkiye’s GDP in 2024 (TÜİK). In SHURA’s 2035 Net Zero scenario, the Marmara price zone uses about 119 TWh a year, a quarter of national demand (474 TWh) and more than a third of everything Türkiye consumed in 2025. The next-largest zones are much smaller: the Aegean–Mediterranean zone uses about 82 TWh, Central Anatolia about 65 TWh and the Konya–Karaman solar belt about 39 TWh. Marmara has 7.7 GW of gas, 7 GW of wind and 1.2 GW of solar in that scenario, so it depends on power flowing in from the rest of the country.

Congestion cost is EPİAŞ’s figure at system marginal prices (SMP). Day-ahead market spend is daily cleared volume multiplied by the price.
Cheap days hide this cost. In May 2026 the day-ahead price averaged 591 TL/MWh (€11). The congestion bill added another 221 TL for every MWh consumed, about 37% on top of the market price. Per MWh of constraint up-regulation, the congestion cost was around 3,000 TL (about €57), five times that month’s average day-ahead price. The cheapest day of the year was 27 May: the price averaged €1.31/MWh, 14 hours cleared at zero, and TEİAŞ still ordered 21.9 GWh of constraint up-regulation. Over 2026 as a whole, the daily constraint volume moves against the price (correlation −0.58) and with the hydro share of generation (+0.69).
Capacity payments are a separate cost and are not included in these figures. In 2024 gas plants received about €195 million from the capacity mechanism for staying available. SHURA’s only link between the two is indirect: with nodal prices, 4 of the 17 supported gas plants would earn enough in the market to no longer need the payment, saving about €41 million a year.

title: One price, two Türkiyes
text:
Already at 2035 levels
Up-regulation for grid constraints reached 6.48 TWh between January and October 2026, which is 2.2% of consumption. In 2025 it was 0.04%, in 2024 0.33%. For 2035, SHURA expects the annual redispatch volume for transmission constraints to be 1.2% of demand in its Reference scenario (5.9 of 479 TWh) and about 3% in its Net Zero scenario (14.6 of 474 TWh). After one wet year, Türkiye is already inside that range. The two numbers are not measured the same way, though: SHURA counts all redispatch, while my 2.2% counts only up-instructions that carry the constraint label.

text:
What SHURA found
SHURA, working with EPRA, simulated Türkiye’s power system in 2035 under three settlement rules: today’s single national price, zonal prices and nodal prices. It ran two scenarios. The Reference scenario has 26 GW of solar and 23 GW of wind; Net Zero has 57 GW of solar and 39 GW of wind. Under nodal pricing almost all congestion is resolved inside the day-ahead market and total welfare rises by 23%. The Net Zero results:

In the report’s words, the welfare gain comes from “more efficient utilization of transmission capacity, a significant reduction in operational balancing instructions (YAL/YAT) costs, and enhanced market transparency”. The gain grows with renewables: in the Reference scenario nodal pricing adds only about 9%. Most of it comes from having locational prices at all. Splitting the country into six zones instead of three adds just 1.2%.
On batteries, the Net Zero scenario assumes 7.2 GW / 28.8 GWh of four-hour storage. Left in the same places, the fleet makes 42% more profit under nodal prices than under the national price, because a single price gives little spread to trade on. If the same 7.2 GW is moved to the nodes with the strongest price signals, profit rises to 48% above the national case. The batteries then sit around İzmir, Bursa, Antalya and Marmara, where daily price swings are widest, and few go east.
The report also looks at Thrace directly. On a representative July day at 14:00 in 2035, Thrace needs 18.1 GW, but the lines from Anatolia can carry 13 GW, so about 5 GW has to come from local plants or from Europe. Thrace’s thermal plants are generally among the expensive ones at the top of the merit order (full report, Figure 60). Under a national price, TEİAŞ curtails cheaper Anatolian output and keeps these plants running through redispatch. When cross-border capacity with Europe is raised to 6.5 GW in a sensitivity case, congestion between Thrace and Anatolia almost disappears. Beyond that point more interconnection helps less and less, and the internal grid becomes the limit.
New lines would not fix this on their own. SHURA’s grid model already includes TEİAŞ’s planned investments plus extra 380 kV and 154 kV reinforcements, and the Net Zero case still ends with 14.6 TWh of congestion. Lines take years to build, solar plants take months. Locational prices would also show where a new line is worth the most, which helps decide where to build next.

title: One price, two Türkiyes
text:
What SHURA recommends
SHURA recommends moving to locational prices in phases, with protection for those who would lose out:

A phased transition. Either nodal prices for generators first, with consumers on a national price until metering improves, or about five or six zones first and nodal prices after a few years of experience.
Support for high-price regions. Targeted help for vulnerable households and strategic industries, which the congestion revenue from locational pricing could fund. Investment incentives and regional development funds could move electricity-intensive industry to low-price regions, or new renewables to high-price ones.
Temporary protection for generators. A revenue stabilisation mechanism for existing plants. Contracts for difference and feed-in premiums can continue, but SHURA says they “should not fully isolate generators from locational price signals”, or siting decisions will not change.
Narrower capacity payments. Broad capacity payments should shrink, and what remains should go to flexibility such as storage.
Hedging tools. Financial Transmission Rights (FTRs) and Congestion Revenue Rights (CRRs), so generators and large consumers can protect themselves against price differences between nodes.
Demand-side flexibility. Consumers in high-price regions would have a reason to shift or cut load at peak, and aggregators could sell that flexibility.
The groundwork. Publish congestion and system-cost data, build the IT for hourly nodal clearing, update the balancing and settlement rules, and coordinate with YEKDEM, YEKA and market coupling with Europe at the Thrace border.

Open congestion data, the first part of point 7, is what made this analysis possible.

title: One price, two Türkiyes
text:
Notes on the data

The constraint label. Every balancing instruction carries a label. Under the Balancing and Settlement Regulation, label 0 is energy balancing, 1 is grid constraints and 2 is ancillary services. I use the label as EPİAŞ publishes it (the “1 kodlu YAL/YAT” columns). Two checks support reading it as the constraint label: since 2018, monthly label-1 up-regulation moves closely with EPİAŞ’s congestion cost (correlation 0.84) while label-0 volumes do not (−0.31), and in months with almost no label-1 up-regulation the congestion cost is close to zero. EPİAŞ has not yet confirmed the definition.
Down-instructions. The matching down-instructions in Anatolia mostly carry label 0. Total down-regulation in May was 3.1 TWh, but only 27 GWh had the constraint label. The label shows the expensive side of redispatch clearly and hides most of the curtailment side.
Congestion cost is EPİAŞ’s published figure by province, at system marginal prices. Its exact definition and reference price are still to be confirmed.
SHURA’s numbers are model results for 2035, with assumptions as of December 2024, not forecasts of today’s market.

title: About
text:
Türkiye’s electricity market publishes a large amount of data. EPİAŞ’s transparency platform carries hourly prices, generation, consumption, balancing and more, and the rules behind them come from EPDK and a long list of regulations and board decisions. In my experience, the numbers are easy to find but harder to turn into a clear picture and interpret. I have found few recent articles or market analyses from an energy economics point of view in Türkiye, especially ones that show how the market has moved over several years. I am designing this site in English first to reach more people, and in later phases I plan to translate it into Turkish, so that my Turkish-speaking colleagues who prefer not to read English can use it too.
TR Power Lab is my attempt to close that gap in the Turkish electricity market. It is an independent project, built on public sources, and it is not affiliated with EPİAŞ, TEİAŞ or EPDK. I learn, experiment and try to share my knowledge and expertise here. I am happy to hear your comments by email or in a message on LinkedIn.

title: Türkiye’s households and the end of the universal electricity subsidy
text: Türkiye is quietly moving from subsidising every household’s electricity to subsidising only low consumption, by lowering the consumption threshold for keeping the subsidised tariff: from 5,000 kWh a year in 2025 to 4,000 in 2026 and 3,000 from 2027. The market is not offering households a better deal than the regulated tariff, as expected. So with the new threshold, 14.7% of households, who can no longer benefit from the regulated tariff, will start carrying the market risk instead.

title: Türkiye’s households and the end of the universal electricity subsidy
text:
Good days of heavy rainfall
2026 has been kind to Türkiye’s electricity bill. Record rainfall filled the dams and hydro output hit an all-time high. In May, the day-ahead price (PTF) averaged 591 TL/MWh (about $13/MWh); in real dollar terms, Ember notes, that was the lowest monthly level since the market opened in 2011. Ember calculated that falling wholesale prices cut the state’s household electricity subsidy by $746 million in January–May.
When I read that report, two things stayed with me. First, the saving is a gap closing, not a bill falling: regulated household tariffs do not follow PTF, and on 4 April 2026 they actually rose by 25%. Second, part of the subsidy drop had nothing to do with renewables. It came from pushing heavy-consuming households out of the subsidised tariff altogether.
That second part is the bigger story, and it is the subject of this piece. Using EPİAŞ transparency data, I look at who left the regulated tariff, when, where, and what they pay now.

title: Türkiye’s households and the end of the universal electricity subsidy
text:
Three thresholds, two directions
A Turkish household’s electricity price is now set by three different thresholds. They are easy to confuse, so it is worth separating them.









Threshold

Eligible consumer (serbest tüketici) limit

The first threshold works inside the regulated tariff. The first ~240 kWh of a monthly bill is charged at a low price and everything above it at a higher one.
The other two pull in opposite directions. The eligibility limit gives a household the right to leave the regulated tariff, and at 500 kWh a year almost every home has it. However, households prefer to stay in the regulated tariff since almost 50% of the bill is subsidised.
The SKTT limit takes away the option to stay. A household loses the regulated tariff when its cumulative use in a calendar year, counted from 1 January, passes 4,000 kWh. The monthly figure of about 333 kWh is only a guide; what counts is the running total, this year or last year. The SKTT then starts on the first day of the third month after the meter reading that crossed the line: a household whose running total passed 4,000 kWh at its 2 June 2026 reading has been billed at the SKTT since 1 September. To return to the regulated tariff, it needs a full calendar year with cumulative use below the next year’s limit.
From 1 January 2027, that line drops to 3,000 kWh, about 250 kWh a month. A household above the line that does not pick a supplier is billed at (PTF + YEKDEM) × 1.05, plus distribution and taxes. EPDK states the purpose plainly: the national tariff carries state support, and households above the limit are meant to buy electricity “at real cost”.



Figure 1. The consumption limit for choosing a supplier and the limit above which the regulated tariff is lost, 2003–2027. The dotted line marks the end of the low tariff tier. Source: EPDK decisions, EMO İzmir, AA, news reports.


One detail matters for what follows. The wires are a regional monopoly: 21 distribution companies, one per region. Retail is not. Each region has one incumbent supplier (görevli tedarik şirketi) that must serve everyone on the regulated tariff and on the SKTT. But an eligible household can sign with any licensed supplier in the country. In practice, the same incumbent group can serve a home in three ways: at the regulated tariff, at the SKTT, or through its own free-market supply company.

title: Türkiye’s households and the end of the universal electricity subsidy
section: Why no supplier can beat the low tier
text:
Why no supplier can beat the low tier
A supplier can only compete on the energy part of the bill. Distribution charges and taxes are regulated and identical whoever sells you the electricity. So the comparison that decides whether switching pays is between two energy prices:

The regulated energy charge. Since 4 April 2026, EPDK’s tariff table sets it at 0.494 TL/kWh for the low tier and 1.896 TL/kWh for the high tier, before taxes.
The market energy cost, (PTF + YEKDEM) × 1.05. This was about 3.2 TL/kWh in January 2026 and about 2.0 TL/kWh in May 2026, when PTF bottomed out.

Even in May, the low tier was roughly a quarter of what the energy cost on the market. No supplier can offer that. The high tier was beaten only in April and May 2026, if at all. Ember, which adds the previous month’s YEKDEM cost, finds the market price fell below it then, after sitting above the residential tariff since June 2021. EPDK, however, bills the SKTT on the same billing period’s average PTF and YEKDEM. On that basis the market cost was about 2.0–2.1 TL/kWh, still just above 1.896.



Figure 2. Top: market energy cost and regulated household energy charges, TL/MWh, before distribution and taxes. Bottom: eligible consumers buying from a supplier, million meters. Dotted lines mark June 2021 (wholesale price rises above the regulated tariff), February 2025 (SKTT reaches households) and January 2026 (4,000 kWh limit). Regulated charges cover 2025–26 only: April 2026 values are EPDK’s tariff table, earlier high-tier values are my estimate. Source: EPİAŞ, EPDK.


This also explains what Ember’s $746 million really is. The subsidy is the gap between the market cost and the tariff, times the subsidised volume. When PTF falls, the gap shrinks and the subsidy shrinks with it, while households keep paying the same bill. Ember’s own decomposition shows a second, quieter effect:

Subsidies fell from $2,015 million to $1,154 million (January–May, 2025 vs 2026, real), largely because record rainfall in January–May 2026 lifted hydro output to an all-time high and pushed wholesale prices down.
$746 million of that came from lower wholesale prices. This is a real saving for the state, which funds the subsidy largely through EÜAŞ.
$228 million came from lowering the SKTT limit. This is not a saving. That cost was moved onto the households pushed out of the tariff.
$113 million went the other way, because the April tariff rise lagged inflation.




Figure 3. Household electricity subsidy, January–May 2025 vs 2026, and the factors behind the change, USD million in real January 2026 prices. Source: Ember (2026).


By my rough estimate, the state paid about half of the full cost of subsidised household electricity in early 2025 and about 40% in early 2026. The rest is the tariff that households pay themselves.

title: Türkiye’s households and the end of the universal electricity subsidy
section: Households switch when they are pushed, not when it pays
text:
Households switch when they are pushed, not when it pays
EPİAŞ publishes a monthly count of eligible meters that buy from a supplier of their choice, split by consumer group. For households, the series tells a clear story.



Figure 4. Eligible consumers buying from a supplier, by consumer group, million meters. Shaded: wholesale price above the regulated tariff (Ember). Source: EPİAŞ, Serbest Tüketici Adedi.


2020 to mid-2021: the test case. Before June 2021, the regulated tariff sat above wholesale prices, so a supplier could undercut it. Commercial users noticed: their switched meters grew from about 0.3 million at the end of 2019 to 1.34 million in October 2021. Households stayed between 8,000 and 12,000 meters nationwide, in a country with about 44 million household subscribers. Households respond little to electricity prices: their demand is inelastic in the short run and they rarely compare suppliers, one of the known weaknesses of retail electricity markets. This is called consumer inertia.
2021 to 2024: the long absence. Once the tariff fell below the market, even commercial users went back to it. Households all but disappeared: 653 household meters had a supplier in December 2024.
2025 to 2026: the push. In February 2025 the SKTT reached households for the first time. It was introduced in 2018 only for the largest industrial users, above 50 GWh a year, and its limit for businesses was cut step by step to 1 GWh in 2022 and 15,000 kWh in 2025 (Figure 1). Switched household meters rose to 300,000 by December 2025 and 789,000 by October 2026. Nothing about the market had become more attractive; for most of 2025 the market energy cost was far above even the high tier. What changed is that the default was taken away.
What about 2017? The series shows 3.38 million households with a supplier in November 2017, collapsing to 44,000 a year later. The same dataset reports a second count, meters registered as eligible but not using the right. For households it rose from 0.17 to 3.28 million in exactly those months, and the sum barely moved.



Figure 5. Household meters registered as eligible consumers: using the right vs not using it, million meters. Source: EPİAŞ, Serbest Tüketici Adedi.


My reading is that these were mostly households moved onto discounted contracts by incumbents’ own retail arms in 2016–17, and moved back when those contracts were unwound. That is a different thing from households shopping around. EPİAŞ labels the second count “Serbest Tüketici Hakkını Kullanmayan Tüketici Sayısı”: in the words of EPİAŞ’s portal guide, meters that have passed the eligibility limit but still buy from their incumbent at EPDK-approved tariffs.

title: Türkiye’s households and the end of the universal electricity subsidy
section: Who picks a supplier, and who doesn’t
text:
Who picks a supplier, and who doesn’t
EPDK expected about 2.5 million households, roughly 6% of household subscribers, to fall under the 4,000 kWh SKTT limit in 2026. At 3,000 kWh from 2027, it expects 6.5 million, or 14.7% of 44.2 million. By October 2026, 789,000 households had signed with a supplier. If EPDK’s estimate holds, about two in three of the households pushed out of the regulated tariff did not pick a supplier and are simply billed at the SKTT price. EPİAŞ’s own count of households that hold the right but do not use it, 2.2 million, is a different group: it was already 2.5 million in December 2024, before the SKTT reached households. The households that did switch are the heaviest users. In September 2026, a household that had switched used about 720 kWh on average, twice the 360 kWh of an eligible household that stayed with its incumbent.
The ones who did pick are concentrated where summers are hot, meaning high AC use, in southern cities like Antalya, Adana and Mersin, as well as in the big economic centres Istanbul, Ankara and İzmir.



Figure 6. Household meters with a supplier contract, top 15 provinces, September 2026. Source: EPİAŞ, İl/İlçe ST Adedi.


Together, the Mediterranean belt holds 46% of the household meters with a supplier contract in September 2026, most of them households that crossed the consumption threshold in 2026. Istanbul’s two sides hold 20%. These are the places where air conditioning pushes a normal family’s use past 333 kWh a month. Because the limit also counts the current year, one hot summer is enough to cross it mid-year and move to the SKTT that autumn.
Households remain a small part of the free market in energy terms. Eligible consumers bought about 170 TWh from suppliers in 2025, and households accounted for 1.9 TWh of it. This is a story about who is protected, not about the size of the competitive market.

title: Türkiye’s households and the end of the universal electricity subsidy
section: The YEKDEM catch: PTF fell 76%, the market price only 36%
text:
The YEKDEM catch: PTF fell 76%, the market price only 36%
The households pushed onto market prices do not pay PTF alone. They pay PTF plus the YEKDEM unit cost, the renewable support surcharge that suppliers pass to every consumer they serve. And YEKDEM moves against PTF.
YEKDEM plants are paid fixed, mostly dollar-based prices. What consumers carry is the difference between those payments and what the plants’ output earns on the market, spread over all supplied energy. When PTF collapses, the payments barely change, the market income disappears, and the unit cost jumps.

Figure 7. Payments to licensed YEKDEM plants and the market value of their output, YEKDEM unit cost and PTF, and hydro generation, 2023–2026. Unlicensed plants are excluded because they enter YEKTOB only from May 2026. Source: EPİAŞ.


Regulated-tariff households never see this; the YEKDEM cost is inside the tariff and covered by the subsidy. The households above 4,000 kWh pay it explicitly, on every kWh.
Germany chose the opposite route. In the middle of the 2022 energy crisis, Germany, the EU’s largest electricity market, removed its renewable surcharge (the EEG-Umlage) from every electricity bill from 1 July 2022. The surcharge had been 3.7 ct/kWh, down from 6.5 ct in 2021, and renewable support has since been paid from a federal fund. That saved a four-person household around €300 a year compared with 2021. Germany moved the cost of renewable support from the bill to the budget, for everyone. Türkiye keeps it on the bill and shields households through the tariff, but only below a consumption limit. The cost is concentrated on the households above it.

title: Türkiye’s households and the end of the universal electricity subsidy
text:
Concerns, risks and opportunities
Consumption is a poor proxy for need. Targeting the subsidy by how much electricity a household uses is simple to administer, but it does not measure wealth. A family of four in Adana with an electric water heater and two air conditioners can pass 3,000 kWh a year, the 2027 limit, without any luxury. A person living alone in a gas-heated 1+1 in Istanbul may use 1,500 kWh. Both may be equally well off, but only the family loses the subsidy. The households most likely to cross the line are large families and homes that have electrified their heating and cooling, which is the direction climate policy wants them to go. (These consumption figures are illustrative, not measured.)
The good days will not last. This year’s low prices rest on full dams. Ember points out that the average capacity factor of Turkish hydro has fallen to 26%, 12 points below 1996–2005. In a dry year, gas fills the gap and PTF rises. The households now on market prices will feel it directly, and the subsidy bill for everyone still below 4,000 kWh will grow again. The policy has moved price risk onto the households it pushed out, at a moment when that risk looks smallest.
The ratchet has already turned again. On 30 October 2026, EPDK cut the household SKTT limit to 3,000 kWh from 1 January 2027: about 250 kWh a month, or a bill of roughly 820 TL. It expects 6.5 million households, 14.7% of all, to fall above it, against about 2.5 million in 2026. The low tier ends at about 2,920 kWh a year, so the line now sits almost exactly where the low tier stops: a household whose use averages more than about 8.2 kWh a day over the year loses the tariff. Exceeding 3,000 kWh in 2026 already counts. The decision also exempts places of worship, martyrs’ families and veterans, and people who depend on electrically powered life support such as dialysis machines and ventilators. That shows targeting by need is possible when the state chooses to do it.
Switching carries its own risks. A household that signs with a supplier gives up some protection. If the supplier goes bankrupt, the household falls back to its incumbent at the last-resort tariff and must sign a new contract within 15 working days. Any deposit it paid the supplier is not protected by EPDK or EPİAŞ. EPİAŞ also runs a process to reverse meters added to a supplier’s portfolio without a signed bilateral contract. Contract prices are also confidential, so EPDK’s online bill calculator cannot check a bilateral bill.
Inertia is a business opportunity. If households move only when pushed, most of the ones pushed will not shop around on their own. That leaves room for services that do it for them: comparison and switching platforms, aggregators that negotiate for groups of households, and suppliers that offer fixed prices to customers who no longer want to carry PTF risk. According to EPDK, EPİAŞ has now built its own system where suppliers’ offers can be compared and agreements made, accessed through e-Devlet and aimed at households first. It goes further than the existing Serbest Tüketici Portalı, where a registered consumer can see their meters, current supplier and incoming supplier requests, but cannot compare offers. Fixed-price household contracts would also give suppliers a reason to hedge. Today suppliers hedge mostly through bilateral contracts with generators and electricity futures on VİOP, because trading is thin on EPİAŞ’s forward market.

title: Natural gas
text:
The spot gas price
The spot gas market (organised by EPİAŞ) trades gas for delivery on the day it is traded and the day after. The reference price, GRF, is the volume-weighted average of its day-ahead and intraday matches. Prices are published in lira per 1,000 standard cubic metres (Sm³). We also show them per megawatt-hour of gas, in euros and in US dollars per MMBtu, the unit of international gas prices. The conversion to energy uses a gross calorific value of 9,155 kcal/Sm³ (1,000 Sm³ = 10.65 MWh), and euro and dollar values use the exchange rate implied by EPİAŞ’s own power prices for each day, so they differ slightly from EPİAŞ’s own conversions. Use the buttons to change the time step, the unit and the range.


                            
                                            




The spot price peaked in September 2022 at 135 EUR/MWh (26,129 TL per 1,000 Sm³), 6.3 times the 2021 average. Over the last twelve months the daily price ranged between 13,721 and 22,738 TL per 1,000 Sm³, and the median change from one day to the next was 0.3%. One possible reason for such small moves is a link to BOTAŞ’s regulated tariff; we have not checked this. In euros the price also changes with the exchange rate.

title: Natural gas
text:
Gas and power prices
Gas-fired plants often set the price of electricity in Türkiye, so the price of gas is a first guide to the price of power. The chart puts the monthly average day-ahead power price (PTF) next to the spot gas price, both in euros per megawatt-hour. Our data does not show which plant sets the price in each hour, so the chart shows how closely the two move together, not that gas sets the price. A power price above the gas price is expected: a gas plant needs more than one megawatt-hour of gas to produce one megawatt-hour of electricity, and has other costs. PTF is also cut off by the price cap and the floor at zero.


                            
                                            




From September 2018 to October 2026 the monthly PTF and the spot gas price have a correlation of 0.94 (1 would mean they always move together); for month-to-month changes it is 0.63. Over the last twelve months alone it is -0.26. The long-run link is consistent with gas plants often setting the price, and the 2021 to 2023 rise is the clearest case, but the relationship is not stable: in May 2026 PTF averaged 11 EUR/MWh with gas at 31 EUR/MWh, when gas supplied 11% of generation. In months with a lot of hydro, wind and solar the gas price tells little about the power price, because other plants set it for many hours.

Gas shippers who are out of balance with the gas system buy or sell the difference at the balancing gas price (BGP). In the data the BGP purchase price is a fixed percentage above the spot reference price and the sale price a fixed percentage below it (yearly medians of the purchase premium: 3% from 2018 to 2022, 5% from 2023). That looks like a rule written into the market design, not a price found by trading; this is still to be confirmed with EPİAŞ. title: Price volatility
text:
Daily price spread
The daily spread is the gap between the most and the least expensive hour of the day-ahead price. It is a first estimate of what a battery could earn from buying in the cheapest hour and selling in the most expensive one, before efficiency losses, fees and the limits of the battery. The second line, the standard deviation, measures how far hourly prices move around the day’s average. Both are monthly averages of daily values. Euros (the default) make years comparable; lira values rise with inflation. The percentage view divides by the month’s average PTF, so it shows spread relative to the price level: a spread of 100% means the gap between the cheapest and the dearest hour equals the average price.

title: Price volatility
section: The cost of being out of balance
text:
The cost of being out of balance
When the system is short, the operator buys extra energy in the balancing market and SMF usually rises above PTF. When it is long, SMF usually falls below PTF. The gap is what a market participant risks by being out of balance in that direction: imbalance prices are built from PTF and SMF. Bars show the monthly average gap, split by system direction, in euros, lira or as a percentage of the month’s average PTF. The percentage is the best way to compare years: a gap of 300 TL/MWh is a large share of a 150 TL/MWh average price and a small share of a 2,000 TL/MWh one.


                            
                                            




The highest short-side gap in percentage terms is May 2026: SMF was 1,528 TL/MWh above PTF while the month’s average PTF was only 591 TL/MWh, so the gap equals 259% of the average price. The lira gap itself was also well above the 290 TL/MWh median of the previous twelve months: this suggests that balancing prices did not fall with the low day-ahead prices. Percentages exaggerate gaps in months with a low average PTF, so read them next to the lira and euro views.

title: Price volatility
text:
Intraday versus day-ahead
The intraday market (GİP) trades the same hours after the day-ahead auction. Its average price (AOF) minus PTF shows whether buying later was cheaper or dearer on average. A gap close to zero means the two markets agree; persistent gaps point to forecasts that changed after the auction, for example for wind and solar.

title: Price volatility
text:
Hours at zero
PTF falls to zero when supply that cannot or will not reduce output, such as run-of-river hydro, wind, solar and must-run plants, exceeds demand. Zero-price hours are a sign of surplus and of the value of storage and flexible demand.

How an entry was checked

Find it. Start from the EPİAŞ market handbook and from a search for the instrument’s title.
